beats.text: Your project is late. The deliverables are not ready. Should you add more people?
Every pair of people on a team needs a communication channel. With N people, there are N times N minus one, over two channels.
Three people: three channels. Four people: six. Five people: ten. Eight people: twenty-eight.
Fred Brooks, in The Mythical Man-Month: adding people to a failing project makes matters worse.
The cost of more communication can outweigh the gain from dividing the work.
So teams stay small. The slides give optimal sizes between three and nine people. A scrum team: three to nine, usually with two to five developers.
Teams also sit inside an organization, in one of three structures.
Project-oriented: each person is dedicated to one project. Performance and schedules improve, but engineers are isolated, and reuse goes down.
Function-oriented: groups by function, and functional managers act as project managers. Clear decisions, but moving people between projects causes delay.
Matrix: people belong to a functional group, but are loaned to projects for their expertise. The main advantage: efficient use of resources.
